To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Kerr nonlinearity is a source of additive Gaussian noise in coherent optical communications systems, and that the variance of the noise has a supra-linear growth with propagation distance.
the variance of the nonlinear distortions is proportional to the signal energy, and that the nonlinear noise accumulation can be accurately modeled with a linear function of propagation distance.

nonlinear transmission distortions are additive and Gaussian, but with a variance that grows with the square of the distance, and can be modeled as a combination of linear and nonlinear noise sources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the statistical properties of nonlinear distortions in optical coherent systems, in order to improve the design of high-capacity optical networks.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in a highly dispersive system, the nonlinear distortions of the optical signal can be described as a Gaussian process.
the nonlinear noise accumulation is the most important factor that limits the transmission distance in coherent optical systems.
nonlinear transmission impairments due to Kerr non-linearity in coherent optical systems can be modeled as a combination of linear and nonlinear Gaussian noise.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the performance of coherent systems can be accurately estimated with a simple model based on the propagation of the signal in an optical fiber with an effective linear dispersion and effective nonlinearity.
nonlinear distortions in highly dispersive optical transmission systems can be modeled as Gaussian noise, with variance that is a nonlinear function of distance.
we have developed a simple model that can be used to predict the performance of highly dispersive coherent optical systems without optical dispersion pre-compensation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, for highly dispersive systems without optical dispersion pre-compensation, Kerr nonlinearity is not an obstacle to long-haul transmission, and can be efficiently mitigated via electronic dispersion compensation.

, in the absence of optical dispersion compensation, nonlinear distortions can be modeled as a Gaussian process, and that the nonlinear noise accumulation is well described by the simple model we propose.

the nonlinear impairments are not a limiting factor for coherent systems over short distances (less than 100 km) but become significant beyond 100 km, especially for high optical signal-to-noise ratios (OSNR) and high launch powers.
